desc: The Aegis cruiser that generated the machine record of the November 2004 encounter and, on the accounts of two of its crew, then lost it. Princeton was operating with Carrier Strike Group 11 off Baja California in the weeks before 14 November 2004 with a freshly upgraded SPY-1B radar and Cooperative Engagement Capability suite. Fravor's sworn statement to House Oversight confirms Princeton had been watching the objects 'on their Aegis combat system for the previous 2 weeks,' descending 'from above 80,000ft ... rapidly down to 20,000ft' and loitering for hours. Princeton's air warfare team, led by Senior Chief Operations Specialist Kevin Day, vectored the VFA-41 section onto the contact that became the Tic Tac intercept. What did not happen next is the story: the Navy's own range fouler report on the incident, released in January 2023, records that 'Reporting terminated at 3rd Fleet, there was no process to share the reporting,' and no Princeton radar or CEC data for the period has ever been produced. Two Princeton crewmen - Day and CEC/Aegis technician Gary Voorhis - have said publicly that recording media were collected by personnel who did not identify themselves within about 48 hours. No document corroborating that collection has surfaced. Princeton is therefore the board's cleanest example of a custody hole: the single richest sensor record of the founding modern case, held by a US warship, and absent from every release since.
